pests.name: Birds and squirrels
pests.note_beginner: Birds and squirrels love sunflower seeds and will strip a ripening seed head fast, sometimes in a day or two. If you want to save the seeds, cover the heads with a paper bag, cheesecloth, or netting once the petals fade. If you are growing sunflowers just for the flowers or to feed wildlife, this is a feature, not a problem.
pests.note_seasoned: The signature sunflower pest at seed stage: birds (finches, jays, blackbirds) and squirrels raid ripening heads and can clear a head quickly. To save seed, cover heads with a paper sack, cheesecloth, or nylon netting secured with a band once the bright petals begin to brown. The same trait makes standing heads valuable as natural bird feeders if seed saving is not the goal, so manage it by intent rather than as pure loss.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny soft insects that cluster on new growth, buds, and the backs of leaves. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap usually handles them, and sunflowers draw ladybugs and other helpers that eat them.
pests.note_seasoned: Soft-bodied sap-feeders on tender growth, buds, and leaf undersides; rarely damaging on vigorous plants and usually checked by the beneficials sunflowers attract. Hose off or treat with insecticidal soap only if populations build on young plants.

pests.name: Sunflower moth and head-clipping weevil
pests.note_beginner: These two pests attack the flower head. Sunflower moth caterpillars tunnel into the developing head and eat the seeds, often leaving webbing. The head-clipping weevil chops the stalk an inch or two below the head, so the whole head droops or drops. Cleaning up old stalks at season end and not planting sunflowers in the same spot every year both help.
pests.note_seasoned: The classic head-infesting pair. Sunflower moth (a small buff-gray moth) lays eggs as heads open; larvae tunnel into the seeds, web the face of the head, and can predispose it to Rhizopus head rot. The sunflower head-clipping weevil (metallic black, long snout) girdles the stalk 1 to 2 inches below the head, dropping it to the ground. Both are managed culturally in the garden: sanitation (destroy spent stalks and dropped heads), crop rotation away from continuous sunflower, and tolerance, since home-scale damage is usually limited.

pests.name: Cutworms
pests.note_beginner: Fat gray or brown caterpillars that hide in the soil and cut off young seedlings at the soil line overnight, leaving them toppled. A cardboard or foil collar around the stem of a new seedling protects it, and clearing weeds before planting helps.
pests.note_seasoned: Stout, smooth gray-to-black caterpillars that sever seedlings at or just below the soil line at night, leaving gaps in the stand. Reduce weedy harborage before sowing, use stem collars on transplants or thinned seedlings, and scout new plantings; damage is a seedling-stage concern that established plants outgrow.

pests.name: Leaf-feeding caterpillars and beetles
pests.note_beginner: Several caterpillars and beetles chew or skeletonize sunflower leaves but rarely do enough damage to need spraying on a healthy plant. Hand-pick if numbers are high.
pests.note_seasoned: A guild of defoliators (thistle caterpillar, woollybears, beet armyworm, sunflower beetle) chew or skeletonize foliage, mostly cosmetic on vigorous garden plants. Hand-pick or spot-treat only at high densities; the plants tolerate substantial leaf loss before bloom is affected.

diseases.name: Sclerotinia (white mold) head and stalk rot
diseases.note_beginner: A fungus that causes a soft, watery rot of the stalk base or the flower head, often with white cottony mold and hard black lumps inside. It thrives in cool, wet conditions and lives in the soil for years, so it is hard to cure. Avoid planting sunflowers where this rot has occurred, give plants room and good drainage, and remove and discard infected plants.
diseases.note_seasoned: Caused by Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, which produces basal stalk rot/wilt, mid-stem rot, and head rot, the most serious sunflower disease. The soilborne sclerotia persist for years and fungicides are largely ineffective, so management is preventive: avoid beds with a white-mold history or recent susceptible broadleaf crops, ensure drainage and airflow, space generously, and remove and destroy infected plants and heads rather than composting them.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A disease that stunts young plants, yellows the leaves with pale blotches on top and white mold underneath, and can kill seedlings in cool, wet soil. Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater seedlings, and pull out badly affected plants. Some seed is sold as mildew-resistant.
diseases.note_seasoned: Caused by Plasmopara halstedii, favored by cool temperatures, high humidity, and waterlogged soil; symptoms include stunting, leaf chlorosis with white downy sporulation on the undersides, and seedling death. It survives in soil for years, so prevention centers on well-drained soil, restrained watering at the seedling stage, resistant hybrids where available, and roguing infected plants; there is no effective rescue treatment once infection takes hold.

diseases.name: Rust
diseases.note_beginner: Small cinnamon-brown spots or bumps on the leaves, usually the undersides, that can spread in warm, wet weather and yellow the foliage. Space plants for airflow, water at the base, and remove badly rusted leaves; it rarely kills a healthy garden plant.
diseases.note_seasoned: Caused by Puccinia helianthi, producing cinnamon-brown uredinial pustules chiefly on lower leaf surfaces, spreading by wind in warm, humid conditions and defoliating heavily in bad years. Manage with spacing and base watering for faster leaf drying, sanitation of infected debris, and resistant cultivars; fungicides exist for severe pressure but are seldom needed in the home garden.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot and powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: Two common leaf problems: Septoria makes brown, angular spots on the leaves, and powdery mildew leaves a white powdery film, both worse in humid, crowded plantings. Give plants room, water the soil rather than the leaves, and clean up fallen debris.
diseases.note_seasoned: Septoria helianthi causes angular brown leaf spots, while powdery mildew lays a white film on foliage in humid, crowded sites; both are foliar and rarely fatal but reduce vigor late in the season. Manage culturally with generous spacing, base watering, morning irrigation if overhead is unavoidable, and removal of infected debris; rotation away from continuous sunflower limits Septoria carryover.
